analysis.one_liner: Requires clear price disclosures in 900-number ads and gives phone customers a formal process to dispute charges billed to their phone bills.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: after a House subcommittee approved a rewritten version (H.R. 3490) in October 1991, the full Energy and Commerce Committee never acted, and no vote was ever taken before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: In the early 1990s, businesses began selling services through 900 numbers, with charges appearing on a customer's phone bill — a system where the obligation hits as soon as someone dials. This bill would have required ads for those services to clearly state what a call costs, disclose the odds when prizes are offered, and require parental consent for callers under 18. It also would have created a formal process for customers to dispute charges billed through their phone company: written notice within 60 days, a carrier investigation within 90 days, no debt collection or bad credit reports while the dispute is open, and forfeiture of the disputed amount if the carrier doesn't follow the rules. It never became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Telephone customers, especially people billed for 900-number services they didn't authorize or didn't get as advertised — the bill would have forced clear pricing in ads up front, given them a set process to dispute charges with strict deadlines for the phone company, barred debt collection and negative credit reports while a dispute was open, and let customers refuse to pay amounts carriers failed to handle properly. Parents of minors and state attorneys general, who would have gained a federal court tool to stop cross-state scams, also benefited.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Customers billed through their phone lines

how_it_helps.text: Ads for 900-number services would have to clearly state the cost, including the per-minute rate, disclose the odds for advertised prizes, and state that callers under 18 need a parent's or guardian's consent.

Customers disputing a phone-billed charge would have 60 days to notify the phone company in writing; the carrier would then have to acknowledge the dispute and either correct the bill or send a written explanation within two billing cycles (no more than 90 days), and could not start collecting the disputed amount while the review was pending.

A carrier that fails to follow the dispute process forfeits its right to collect the disputed amount and any late fees, giving customers real leverage; for goods claimed to be undelivered, the carrier cannot call the bill correct unless it confirms delivery.

While a dispute is open, vendors and carriers could not threaten or report the customer's account as delinquent to third parties without also disclosing that the amount is disputed, and any resolution would have to be reported to those parties.

Customers who in good faith tried to resolve a problem with the vendor could raise their claims and defenses against the phone company seeking payment, so they would not be stuck paying a bill for a bad purchase just because it arrived on their phone statement.

State attorneys general could sue in federal court on behalf of their residents to stop violators and win damages, giving states a direct enforcement tool against scams that operate across state lines.

analysis.who_pays: Pay-per-call (900-number) vendors and telemarketers, who would have faced mandatory disclosure rules; and telephone companies, which would have been placed under Federal Trade Commission jurisdiction for this purpose, required to open their vendor arrangements to FTC inspection, and made responsible for investigating and correcting billing errors — losing the ability to collect disputed charges they mishandled.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds real compliance costs: carriers must forward and investigate disputes on deadlines, provide documentary evidence on request, and forfeit the disputed amount and late fees if they miss the requirements — costs that small carriers and vendors would bear and might pass through to customers.
The bill's protections depend entirely on FTC rulemaking within 270 days of enactment and FTC enforcement afterward; a slow or underfunded FTC would leave the statutory rights largely on paper.

Extending FTC jurisdiction over communications common carriers for these purposes creates overlapping oversight with existing federal and state telephone regulation, which the bill only partially harmonizes by letting the FTC exempt classes of transactions already covered by substantially similar state rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to phone customers are real and practical: clear prices before dialing, a deadline-driven dispute process, and protection from collection and credit damage while a charge is contested [S3]. The costs are modest and mostly regulatory — carriers and vendors face recordkeeping and investigation duties, and the FTC must run a rulemaking within 270 days [S3]. The bill is not badly designed; it exempts normal phone service, preserves stronger state laws, and uses the existing FTC enforcement machinery rather than creating new agencies [S3]. Its main weakness is that it depended on FTC rulemaking and FTC enforcement capacity to deliver results, and it never got far enough to be tested or amended by a full committee.

outcome.mechanism: A House subcommittee marked up the bill in August 1991 and forwarded a rewritten version, H.R. 3490, to the full committee that October, but the full committee never took it up and no vote was ever held before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Al Swift introduced the bill on July 9, 1991, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On July 22, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials, which held a consideration and mark-up session on August 1, 1991.
On October 3, 1991, the subcommittee forwarded a clean bill, H.R. 3490, to the full committee in lieu of the original.
The bill had no cosponsors, and the record shows no further action — no full committee markup, no floor vote, and no Senate activity — before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Phone companies and 900-number operators were better off: without a law on the books, they continued charging customers' phone bills without mandatory price disclosures, formal dispute deadlines, or forfeiting collection rights when they mishandled a dispute. Phone customers who disputed charges kept facing the older, weaker rules.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew recorded opposition or a vote; it had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors [S4], so no partisan pattern appears in the record.

industries.note: Mandatory price, odds, and parental-consent disclosures would curb the abusive practices the bill's own findings describe, but the same findings argue a uniform federal framework would build the consumer confidence a legitimate pay-per-call marketplace needs to grow. For consumers, the industry's gain from legitimacy sits alongside its loss of freedom to run confusingly priced, prize-baited ads.

Carriers — historically exempt from FTC jurisdiction — would be forced to open their vendor arrangements to FTC inspection, process billing disputes on fixed deadlines, and forfeit disputed charges they mishandle. In exchange, the bill gives them a standardized dispute framework that legitimates the phone bill as a collection channel for third-party vendors, which is a revenue stream carriers profit from.

Rather than banning telephone-billed sales, the bill builds a permanent federal disclosure and dispute-resolution framework around them, treating phone billing as a lasting marketplace channel that consumers would keep paying into — with protections attached.
